opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think the skepticism was completely understandable. Around 2015 I was coming out of computer graphics, where my PhD work was on physics-based character animation: teaching simulated characters to walk, swim, or ride a bicycle using optimization and learning. When I said these methods could change real robotics, many roboticists reasonably asked, "Isn't that just animation? It only has to look right on screen."

There's real truth in that. In graphics, if a motion looks plausible, you've succeeded. A real robot has to deal with friction you didn't model exactly, motor delays, sensor noise, slight differences in mass, and the floor isn't perfectly flat. A controller that works beautifully in simulation can fail within seconds on hardware. That's the sim-to-real gap, and in 2015 it was a very solid wall. Most serious robotics people believed you had to hand-engineer controllers carefully, and that learning in simulation was mostly a toy.

So I didn't take the skepticism as hostility. I took it as a precise statement of the problem I needed to solve. My bet was that the core ideas from graphics — fast physics simulation, large-scale optimization, letting an agent learn through enormous amounts of trial and error — were actually the right foundation. The missing piece was closing the gap: making the simulator more faithful where it matters, identifying the robot's real parameters, randomizing the simulation so the policy becomes robust, and designing controllers that don't overfit to one perfect virtual world.

Also, I was an outsider. When you come from a different field, people naturally wonder whether you understand their hard problems. The only real answer to that is results. When you can train a legged robot in simulation and then have it walk on the real hardware, the conversation changes very quickly.

Today, training in simulation and transferring to the real world is almost the default approach for locomotion, and increasingly for manipulation. But I don't think the skeptics were wrong to doubt it back then. Their doubts pointed exactly at the hardest parts, and working through those was what made the approach actually succeed.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Tan was coming out of computer graphics, where his PhD work focused on character animation, and connects being an outsider from another field to others’ doubts.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the skepticism was completely reasonable, and honestly, if I had been sitting on the other side of the table, I might have been skeptical too.

You have to remember what robotics looked like in 2015. The dominant approach was model-based: you write down the dynamics, you do careful system identification, you design a controller analytically, and you hope the real robot matches the equations. The idea that someone from computer graphics, someone who had spent years making virtual characters walk and swim and fall over in animated films, could just come in and say "we'll train things in simulation and then put them on real hardware" sounded naive. People would say, very politely, that simulation is where you go when you don't have a real robot. The joke was that simulations are doomed to succeed.

And the deeper objection was the reality gap. In graphics, if your simulated character's gait is slightly wrong, nobody gets hurt. The audience just sees something that looks plausible. In robotics, a small mismatch in friction, in motor latency, in the mass distribution of a leg, and your quadruped falls on its face. So the roboticists weren't being closed-minded. They were pointing at a real problem that I didn't yet have a convincing answer to.

What I had was more of a conviction than a proof. I had seen in graphics how much you could learn from physics-based simulation when you had essentially unlimited data and could run things thousands of times faster than real time. I believed the gap was an engineering problem, not a fundamental barrier. But belief isn't an argument you can make in a review meeting.

So I took the skepticism as a to-do list, really. Every objection became a research question. How do you make simulation faithful enough? How do you make policies robust to the parts you can't make faithful? That led directly to the work on sim-to-real for legged locomotion, domain randomization, actuator modeling, and later the learning-from-real-world work. The fact that those methods now feel almost standard is, in a strange way, the best answer I could give to the people who doubted it in 2015. They weren't wrong about the difficulty. They were just wrong about whether it could be overcome.

r001.rationale: The candidate ties the skepticism to Tan coming from computer graphics and proposing to apply simulation-based methods to robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think the skepticism was understandable. In graphics, a simulation can be successful if it looks convincing. In robotics, the question is whether it captures the physics accurately enough that something you learn in simulation will actually work on a real machine. Those are very different standards.

A robot has to deal with friction, contact, delays, and uncertainty. If your simulation gets those things wrong, the robot may fail even though everything looked great on the screen. So the concern was legitimate: how much could methods developed for graphics really help?

My optimism was that simulation could let us experiment and learn at a scale that would be very difficult with physical robots alone. It didn’t have to reproduce every detail perfectly to be useful. But that was something we needed to demonstrate on real robots. The skepticism put the focus on the right question: could we make the transfer work?

r001.rationale: The response discusses skepticism about whether graphics methods could help robotics, but does not attribute that skepticism to Jie Tan’s predominantly graphics background.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the skepticism was understandable. In graphics, a simulation succeeds if the motion looks convincing. In robotics, it has to be accurate enough that a real machine can act on it. A small error in contact or friction can mean the difference between walking and falling.

So when I talked about bringing graphics methods into robotics in 2015, the concern was: even if you can train something in simulation, why should it work in the real world? That was a fair question. I saw simulation as a way to let robots learn through much more trial and error than we could afford on hardware. But we had to demonstrate that those skills could transfer. The ambition alone wasn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response explains skepticism as concern that simulation-trained skills might not transfer accurately to real robots. It does not attribute the skepticism to Tan’s predominantly graphics background.
